content: National censuses and decentralized monitoring systems are often used to collect data on sanitation and hygiene. Household surveys, conducted by national statistical authorities or supported externally through initiatives like the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) and the Demographic and Health Survey (DHS), are typically carried out every four to five years. These surveys provide valuable information at the national and sometimes sub-national levels but often lack the granularity needed for detailed local planning. This training should include the use of standardized tools, such as illustrations that classify technologies as improved or unimproved, to enhance data consistency. Environmental health officers also play a critical role in monitoring sanitation and hygiene behaviors at the individual, utility, or sub-national levels. They support local authorities and health workers in assessing the containment, conveyance, treatment, and safe disposal or reuse of waste. When lapses are identified, corrective actions should be initiated with the responsible individuals or institutions. Given practical constraints, only a limited number of indicators can be monitored. Risk assessments should identify critical control points for regular monitoring. At the global level, sanitation is tracked using the indicator of the proportion of the population using safely managed sanitation services. This is defined as the use of improved sanitation facilities that are not shared with other households and where excreta are either treated and disposed of on-site, stored temporarily and transported to off-site treatment, or transported via sewer systems for off-site treatment. National monitoring systems should include core global indicators as a minimum, along with additional elements relevant to national contexts, such as service levels, settings, sub-populations, and enabling environments. Environmental health officers are instrumental in collecting data on sanitation facilities, their usage, and the effectiveness of on-site treatment or the emptying and transport of fecal sludge. They also assess the extent of untreated sewage leakage or overflow, the compliance of sludge and sewage treatment with national standards, and the effectiveness of community engagement in sanitation efforts. Data collection methods include inspections of dwellings and buildings, customer surveys, and information from operators, licensing authorities, or regulatory bodies. For example, data on the emptying and transport of on-site facilities and untreated sewage overflow can be gathered from customers and operators. The effectiveness of sludge and sewage treatment should be verified through occasional sampling and independent laboratory analysis. Service providers should report specified monitoring information, subject to inspection by environmental health authorities, with inspection frequency based on trust levels and potential hazards from non-compliance. Community engagement in sanitation requires discussions with local officials and community members. Comprehensive sanitary inspection forms have been developed to assist environmental health officers in this process. These data, combined with information on open defecation, enable assessments of sanitation beyond Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) definitions and inform planning. Incentives and resources for data collection may be limited, but accountability mechanisms, such as linking data collection to government budget releases, can encourage monitoring efforts. Part of these budgets should cover monitoring costs. To fully perform their roles, environmental health staff require training to manage specialists and contractors and advocate for sufficient resources for sanitation behavior change. Frontline staff, such as extension and community outreach officers, should also receive formal training. Monitoring relevant health and epidemiological data, such as routine surveillance at healthcare facilities, can help identify the public health burden of poor sanitation. Special attention should be given to ensuring that women, girls, and vulnerable groups are adequately served. Sanitation planning and implementation must be coordinated with other basic services, such as water supply, drainage, and solid waste management, particularly in high-density urban environments. Local governments should take overall responsibility for sanitation, even when service provision is delegated to utility companies or private sector entities. Sanitation must be explicitly included in planning and budgeting processes, with recognition of nationally and locally established service level targets. Coordination groups at the city or district level, involving senior representatives from relevant departments and stakeholders, should meet periodically to align activities. Behavior change is integral to achieving sanitation and hygiene goals. Strategies should address multiple behaviors along the sanitation service chain, as infrastructure alone cannot deliver desired public health outcomes. Monitoring systems should leverage available frontline staff in communities to increase sustainability and reduce costs. A georeferenced database of sanitation facilities and their conditions can aid planning, management, and the design of sanitation promotion strategies. Sanitation services must be tailored to the physical, social, and economic conditions of each area. Assessments should identify inadequacies in existing sanitation systems, risks to public health, and factors contributing to these issues. Stakeholders, including users, should be actively engaged in the assessment process to develop feasible solutions with the greatest public health impact. These solutions should address hardware, sanitation promotion, institutional development, legislation, regulation, and financing. Sanitation services may be provided by the private sector, utility companies, local governments, or a combination of these. Public investment is often required for major infrastructure, such as sewerage systems, which may be managed directly by the public sector, utility companies, or leased to private operators. Decentralized sanitation systems, such as small sewerage systems and fecal sludge transfer facilities, are increasingly needed in urban areas. Community engagement can help overcome resistance to these systems. Capacity building is essential for formalizing sanitation services. Partnerships with academic institutions, NGOs, or social enterprises can support technical development and adaptation. Training for service providers should include business and technical skills to improve efficiency and sustainability. Mechanisms such as joint representation to financial institutions, small grants, equipment leasing, and results-based financing can help small enterprises access resources. Improved sanitation services often compete with traditional unsafe services. Traditional providers should be encouraged to transition to improved services, leveraging their knowledge of wastewater and user behavior. Engaging with these providers early can make them part of the solution rather than the problem. Financing sanitation services requires a mix of user fees, public funding, and subsidies. Tariff structures should reflect users' ability to pay to prevent exclusion of poor households. In urban areas, sanitation fees can be integrated into water tariffs or local taxes. In rural areas, government budgets may be the primary funding source for sanitation promotion and safe toilet use. Subsidies may be needed for vulnerable households or to address the costs of improving toilets for mechanical emptying. Sustained promotion programs are necessary to foster new norms of sanitation behavior. Marketing and behavior change campaigns require substantial resources and should be based on adequate research among target groups. Commercial entities may supply various sanitation services, such as hardware, public toilets, and desludging. Competition can lower prices, making services more accessible while increasing sales volumes. Container-based sanitation services are emerging as an option, particularly in high-density urban areas. Marketing is crucial to delivering affordable services, and subsidies may be required for the poorest households. Regular scheduled desludging programs can help spread demand throughout the year. Resource recovery, such as biogas or compost, can offset some treatment costs but rarely covers the full cost. Finally, fostering an efficient sanitation services market involves creating platforms where customers can find providers and provide feedback. Databases of toilets and sanitation facilities are essential for monitoring and planning.
